Package-manager supply-chain control bypass via pnpm minimumReleaseAge=0 AIInstallation High
Hunts for npm/pnpm/yarn install invocations that explicitly set minimumReleaseAge=0 on the command line, disabling pnpm 11's default new-package quarantine window. This is the exact bypass the article cites (an AI coding agent running `pnpm install --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`), which re-opens the exposure window during which freshly published malicious packages are most dangerous. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim code block `pnpm install --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`; the value `=0` is the high-fidelity discriminator (legitimate hardening sets a positive minute count like 1440/10080, never 0). Cross-checked against pnpm's own supply-chain docs and a pnpm 11 write-up confirming 1440-minute default and that 0 disables the control. Cross-checked against: • https://pnpm.io/supply-chain-security • https://cybersecuritynews.com/pnpm-11-turns-on-minimum-release-age/ • https://pnpm.io/settings
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build agent deliberately running with minimumReleaseAge=0 to always resolve latest dependencies
  • Developer pulling a legitimate security hotfix published inside the quarantine window
  • AI coding agent self-unblocking on a needed dependency (the article's own sanctioned-but-risky scenario)
  • Container image build step that bootstraps a monorepo and disables the delay for speed
  • Internal package-publish smoke tests that install their own just-published artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line, parent process, and user/host. Determine if it ran under an interactive developer session or a CI/build agent, and whether the install pulled any package published within the last 24h. 2) Contain: if non-sanctioned, kill the install, quarantine the host's node_modules/lockfile delta, and block the resolved package versions pending review; require minimumReleaseAge to remain at the org default. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for newly installed packages (FileWritten under node_modules), outbound connections from node.exe to non-registry domains, and any postinstall script execution (node/npm spawning cmd/powershell) in the minutes after install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "minimumReleaseAge"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)minimumReleaseAge\s*=\s*0(\D|$)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "minimumReleaseAge"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)minimumReleaseAge\s*=\s*0(\D|$)"
| where not(Account endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — npm v12 delivers one of the biggest security improvements in years
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] axios RAT Windows payload drop (6202033.vbs/.ps1, ProgramData\wt) during npm install · [LLM] Shai-Hulud npm preinstall Bun bootstrap (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] axios npm RAT C2 beacon to UNC1069 infra (142.11.206.73 / sfrclak.com) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TruffleHog secret-scan spawned by npm/node install (Shai-Hulud credential harvest) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
axios npm RAT C2 beacon to UNC1069 infra (142.11.206.73 / sfrclak.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the hard-coded command-and-control infrastructure used by the March 2026 axios/plain-crypto-js supply-chain RAT (UNC1069). Any internal host reaching 142.11.206.73 or resolving sfrclak.com after an npm install is a confirmed post-install RAT beacon. Rationale: Anchors on the dedicated C2 IP 142.11.206.73 and domain sfrclak.com, confirmed by Google Threat Intelligence, Microsoft and SANS as UNC1069's axios-campaign infrastructure (port 8000, 60s beacon) — a pure IOC match with effectively no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sans.org/blog/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise-malicious-packages-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the axios sample in a malware sandbox that egresses to the live C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning tooling actively connecting to the IOC IP to fingerprint it
  • Internal honeypot or deception host deliberately reaching the IOC
  • IP later reassigned to a benign hosting provider months after takedown
  • Proxy log replays / SIEM test harness injecting the IOC for rule validation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source host and the initiating process for the connection (DeviceNetworkEvents InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine); confirm an npm/node install ran in the prior minutes. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, block 142.11.206.73 and sfrclak.com at egress, and kill the beaconing process tree. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same host for %TEMP%\6202033.vbs/.ps1 and %PROGRAMDATA%\wt drops, enumerate installed package-lock for axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js@4.2.1, and rotate any npm/SSH/cloud tokens present on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73" or RemoteUrl has "sfrclak.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "142.11.206.73" or DestinationHostName has "sfrclak.com" or RequestURL has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT Windows payload drop (6202033.vbs/.ps1, ProgramData\wt) during npm install AIInstallation High
Hunts the Windows-specific payload files written by the March 2026 axios supply-chain RAT — %TEMP%\6202033.vbs, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1 and the %PROGRAMDATA%\wt staging dir — plus the campaign's malware SHA256 set. Surfaces the install-time RAT drop before C2 is established. Rationale: Uses the exact Windows artifact names (6202033.vbs/.ps1, %PROGRAMDATA%\wt) documented by SANS/Microsoft plus the article's pre-extracted SHA256 set; file names + hashes are high-fidelity and effectively never collide with benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sans.org/blog/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise-malicious-packages-remote-access-trojan • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://snyk.io/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-supply-chain-attack-delivers-cross-platform/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.005 T1059.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR writing a quarantine copy of the payload under a vendor cache path (hash match)
  • Windows Terminal or other vendor unpacking a benign 'wt' folder under ProgramData (path clause only)
  • DFIR analyst copying the captured sample onto an investigation host
  • A benign internal script coincidentally numbered 6202033 (extremely unlikely given exact name+ext)
  • SIEM/EDR detection-validation harness planting the IOC files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","senseir.exe") and FolderPath has "Quarantine")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine) — node.exe/npm.exe/bun.exe writing these files confirms install-time drop, not AV quarantine. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, quarantine the dropped files, and kill any wscript/powershell process executing 6202033.vbs/.ps1. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for 142.11.206.73/sfrclak.com from the same host, check %PROGRAMDATA%\wt for the persistent RAT binary and any scheduled task/Run key pointing at it, and audit the project's package-lock for axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js@4.2.1.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1")
    or SHA256 in ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09","b74caeaa75e077c99f7d44f46daaf9796a3be43ecf24f2a1fd381844669da777","dc67467a39b70d1cd4c1f7f7a459b35058163592f4a9e8fb4dffcbba98ef210c","4b2399646573bb737c4969563303d8ee2e9ddbd1b271f1ca9e35ea78062538db","62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0","f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068","cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd","a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
    or (FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\wt\" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1")
    or TargetFileSHA256 in ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09","b74caeaa75e077c99f7d44f46daaf9796a3be43ecf24f2a1fd381844669da777","dc67467a39b70d1cd4c1f7f7a459b35058163592f4a9e8fb4dffcbba98ef210c","4b2399646573bb737c4969563303d8ee2e9ddbd1b271f1ca9e35ea78062538db","62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0","f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068","cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd","a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
    or TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\wt\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: axios npm RAT Windows payload drop (6202033.vbs/.ps1, ProgramData wt)
id: 7a1f0c44-2b9e-4d51-8c3a-9e6b2d4f1c12
description: Detects the Windows payload files written by the March 2026 axios/plain-crypto-js supply-chain RAT during npm install.
references:
  - https://www.sans.org/blog/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise-malicious-packages-remote-access-trojan
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.005
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\6202033.vbs'
      - '\6202033.ps1'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\ProgramData\wt\'
  condition: selection_name or selection_path
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\6202033.vbs OR *\6202033.ps1 OR *\6202033.VBS OR *\6202033.PS1) OR @TargetFilename:(*\ProgramData\wt\* OR *\programdata\wt\*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(6202033\.(vbs|ps1)$|\\ProgramData\\wt\\)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="6202033.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="6202033.ps1" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\wt\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_guid
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="6202033.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="6202033.ps1" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\wt\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_guid

Shai-Hulud npm preinstall Bun bootstrap (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud 2.0 / Mini Shai-Hulud worm bootstrap: an npm lifecycle script invoking node against setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js / bun_installer.js / environment_source.js, or a Bun runtime spawned as a child of node/npm. Bun appearing inside a Node install is the campaign's signature anomaly. Rationale: Anchors on the exact Shai-Hulud preinstall script filenames confirmed by Datadog/ReversingLabs/Zscaler plus the anomalous 'bun spawned by node/npm' relationship the worm relies on to evade Node-focused defenses. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-v2-poses-risk-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately uses the Bun runtime in a Node monorepo (e.g. TanStack tooling) invoking bun via node wrappers
  • A developer who genuinely named a setup helper setup_bun.js for a real Bun migration
  • CI agents bootstrapping Bun as part of a sanctioned toolchain
  • Container image builds that install Bun under node during npm/pnpm steps
  • Local benchmarking comparing Bun vs Node started from an npm script
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tanstack","bunfig.toml") or FolderPath has @"\.bun\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent npm install — confirm the script came from node_modules (a dependency) rather than the repo's own committed tooling. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the bun/node tree, and freeze the developer's npm and GitHub tokens. Step 3 (hunt): Look on the same host for TruffleHog execution, outbound pushes to attacker GitHub repos, and any newly-published packages from the maintainer's account; scan node_modules for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js to scope the blast radius.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","bun_installer.js","environment_source.js")
   or (FileName =~ "bun.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","cmd.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","bun_installer.js","environment_source.js")
   or (ActingProcessName has "bun" and ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud npm preinstall Bun bootstrap scripts
id: b2d8e5a1-6c47-4f93-8a2b-1d3f9c7e4b22
description: Detects the Shai-Hulud worm bootstrap scripts (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js / bun_installer.js / environment_source.js) or a Bun runtime spawned by node/npm during install.
references:
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
  - https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_script:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'setup_bun.js'
      - 'bun_environment.js'
      - 'bun_installer.js'
      - 'environment_source.js'
  selection_bun:
    Image|endswith: '\bun.exe'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
  condition: selection_script or selection_bun
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@CommandLine:(*setup_bun.js* OR *bun_environment.js* OR *bun_installer.js* OR *environment_source.js*) OR (@Image:(*\bun.exe OR *\Bun.exe) AND @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm.exe)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(setup_bun\.js|bun_environment\.js|bun_installer\.js|environment_source\.js)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*setup_bun.js*" OR Processes.process="*bun_environment.js*" OR Processes.process="*bun_installer.js*" OR Processes.process="*environment_source.js*" OR (Processes.process_name="bun.exe" AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","cmd.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*setup_bun.js*" OR Processes.process="*bun_environment.js*" OR Processes.process="*bun_installer.js*" OR Processes.process="*environment_source.js*" OR (Processes.process_name="bun.exe" AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","cmd.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| sort - lastTime
TruffleHog secret-scan spawned by npm/node install (Shai-Hulud credential harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts TruffleHog being executed as a child of node/npm/bun — the Shai-Hulud worm's credential-harvesting step that sweeps SSH keys, GitHub/npm tokens and cloud credentials during install. TruffleHog launched by a package manager (rather than CI/pre-commit) is the article-specific signal. Rationale: Anchors on TruffleHog (the Shai-Hulud secret-sweeper named by Datadog/ReversingLabs) constrained to a node/npm/bun parent, distinguishing worm-driven credential theft from sanctioned CI/pre-commit secret scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A husky/lint-staged pre-commit hook running TruffleHog as a child of node (legitimate secret scanning)
  • A developer manually running trufflehog via an npm script for a security review
  • CI runners executing TruffleHog through a Node-based pipeline wrapper
  • Security tooling that wraps TruffleHog in a node CLI installed org-wide
  • A package that legitimately vendors TruffleHog for its own scanning feature
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("husky","lint-staged","pre-commit",".git/hooks"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the trufflehog invocation originated from a committed dev hook (husky/lint-staged in the repo) or from inside node_modules / a lifecycle script — the latter is malicious. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the process tree, and immediately rotate all secrets reachable from that workstation (SSH keys, GitHub/npm/cloud tokens). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with Bun bootstrap scripts (setup_bun.js) and outbound activity to attacker-controlled GitHub repos or 142.11.206.73/sfrclak.com on the same host, and review the maintainer's recent npm publishes for worm propagation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","bun","cmd","powershell","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process Actions on Objectives High
Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore.json, MetaMask, Exodus, Atomic, Phantom data.
ATT&CKT1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\", @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\", @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\", @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\",
                                  @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\",
                                  @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\",
                                  @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe",
                                  "electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

status: experimental

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

SPECTRALVIPER DLL side-load: IntelAudioService.exe (renamed dtlupdate.exe) loads DtlCrashCatch.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER side-load chain where a renamed legitimate signed binary (dtlupdate.exe masquerading as IntelAudioService.exe) loads the malicious DtlCrashCatch.dll loader. Article-specific because both the masqueraded EXE name and the unique malicious DLL name are named IOCs from the FireAnt MetaKit campaign. Rationale: DtlCrashCatch.dll and the dtlupdate.exe→IntelAudioService.exe masquerade are named in the cybersecuritynews/gbhackers write-ups of the FireAnt SPECTRALVIPER chain; the DLL name is unique enough that any load/write is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/oceanlotus-apt-compromises-fireant-metakit/ • https://gbhackers.com/oceanlotus-targets-stock-investors/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named Intel audio service binary loading an unrelated vendor DLL (the pair clause only — the DtlCrashCatch.dll clause has no benign match)
  • Security-vendor sandbox/detonation hosts replaying the sample
  • IR/forensics team copying the DLL onto an analysis VM triggering FileCreate
  • Backup/restore agent rehydrating quarantined files
Suppression filter
| where not (LoaderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Intel\\" and Module !~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loader's path and signer — genuine Intel binaries live under Program Files\Intel; a DtlCrashCatch.dll under a user/Temp/AppData path is malicious. Pull the LoaderSHA1 and cross-check against the campaign hash list. 2) Contain: isolate the host in Defender/Falcon, kill the IntelAudioService.exe/dtlupdate.exe process tree, and quarantine DtlCrashCatch.dll. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe network egress and connections to financemachinelearning.com and the campaign C2 IPs; check whether setup.exe (FireAnt MetaKit updater) wrote the DLL.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll" or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "IntelAudioService.exe" and FileName endswith ".dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Loader=InitiatingProcessFileName, LoaderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoaderSHA1=InitiatingProcessSHA1, Module=FileName, ModulePath=FolderPath, ModuleSHA1=SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 communication to FireAnt-campaign domains/IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on host connections or DNS lookups to the SPECTRALVIPER command-and-control domains and IPs used across the FireAnt MetaKit and construction-firm intrusions (2024-2026). Article-specific: every indicator is a confirmed campaign C2 from the ESET report and Table 2. Rationale: Uses the confirmed SPECTRALVIPER C2 domains (financemachinelearning.com etc. from Table 2) and the resolved IPs; multiple second sources (Elastic, ESET, CyberSecurityNews) attribute these to the same campaign, so no single-source-only IOCs were shipped. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oceanlotus-hits-vietnam-investors-with.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/oceanlotus-targets-stock-investors-and-construction-firm-with-spectralviper-backdoor
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/IOC scanners or TIP enrichment jobs resolving the domains for validation
  • Sinkholed domains post-takedown resolving to a research sinkhole IP
  • A shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a benign tenant (IP clause stale)
  • Security researcher detonating samples on a corporate analysis subnet
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Windows Defender")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName making the connection — OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe, IntelAudioService.exe, setup.exe or an unexpected process strongly confirms SPECTRALVIPER; note whether the URL contains /apparatus/wind/twig/statement.html. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the C2 domains/IPs at proxy and firewall, and revoke any cached creds from that host. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same destinations over 90 days, look for the DtlCrashCatch.dll side-load and setup.exe hashes, and check FireAnt MetaKit install footprint org-wide.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
let c2IPs = dynamic(["139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2IPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA1, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
let c2IPs = dynamic(["139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);
union
(ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (c2IPs) | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DstIpAddr, IndicatorType="ip"),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (c2Domains) | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DnsQuery, IndicatorType="domain")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FireAnt MetaKit trojanized setup.exe (SPECTRALVIPER downloader) by known hash AIDelivery High
Alerts on execution of the trojanized FireAnt MetaKit installer (setup.exe) variants that delivered SPECTRALVIPER, matched on the 20 campaign SHA1 hashes. Targets the supply-chain delivery step rather than later C2, giving earliest-possible detection. Rationale: The 20 setup.exe SHA1 hashes are the article's pre-extracted IOC list, corroborated by CyberSecurityNews as the FireAnt MetaKit SPECTRALVIPER downloader variants; hash equality is exact and zero-FP outside the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/oceanlotus-apt-compromises-fireant-metakit/ • https://gbhackers.com/oceanlotus-targets-stock-investors/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sandbox/CI detonation hosts executing the collected samples
  • Security-team threat-hunt VM running the IOC for validation
  • EDR re-scan of a previously quarantined file generating a synthetic process record
  • Hash collision is cryptographically implausible for SHA1 here — no benign FP expected from the hash itself
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually ran FireAnt MetaKit and capture parent process + user; verify the file path (was it served by the FireAnt updater?). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the binary, and pull memory before reboot to capture the injected SPECTRALVIPER in OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe. 3) Hunt: enumerate all FireAnt MetaKit installs org-wide, search for the side-load DLL DtlCrashCatch.dll and connections to financemachinelearning.com, and scope which update versions were pulled in the Oct 2025-Mar 2026 window.

SPECTRALVIPER injected OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe beaconing (Cookie-header C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts SPECTRALVIPER's post-injection beacon: the masqueraded OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe (injection target) making public outbound connections, or any host reaching the hardcoded beacon path /apparatus/wind/twig/statement.html. Catches the C2 stage even if domain/IP infrastructure rotates, by pivoting on the injected host process and unique URI. Rationale: Pivots on the named injection target OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe (cybersecuritynews) plus the hardcoded beacon URI /apparatus/wind/twig/statement.html — a legit OneDrive sync uses OneDrive.exe, so this process name reaching public C2 is high-fidelity and survives infrastructure rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/oceanlotus-apt-compromises-fireant-metakit/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1055 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine third-party app legitimately named OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe (uncommon — real binary is OneDrive.exe) hitting a benign CDN
  • Web-proxy URL-decode artifacts matching the statement.html path on an unrelated site (the full /apparatus/wind/twig/ path makes this very unlikely)
  • Internal vuln scanner probing the beacon URI during an IOC sweep
  • Microsoft OneDrive telemetry endpoints if the host process name is spoofed but destination is legitimately Microsoft (excluded by C2 dest clause in proxy variant)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\OneDrive" and Dests has_any (dynamic(["13.107.42.12","13.107.6.171"])))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe path and signer — a real OneDrive sync process is OneDrive.exe under AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive; an unsigned/oddly-pathed OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe with public egress is the injected SPECTRALVIPER. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture a memory image to recover the injected payload, then block the C2 and kill the process. 3) Hunt: pivot the host for the DtlCrashCatch.dll side-load and setup.exe hashes, and search proxy logs org-wide for the /apparatus/wind/twig/statement.html URI and Cookie-header beacons to the campaign domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
     or RemoteUrl has "/apparatus/wind/twig/statement.html"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), Dests=make_set(RemoteIP, 50), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl, 50), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "/apparatus/wind/twig/statement.html" or UrlOriginal has "apparatus/wind/twig/statement.html"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpUserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10520", "CVE-2026-10523")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10520", "CVE-2026-10523")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
