Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious 'postmark-mcp' MCP server package present/executing on developer endpoints
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GlassWorm Stage-2 C2 beacon to Vultr-hosted command-and-control IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Malicious 'postmark-mcp' MCP server package present/executing on developer endpoints AIDelivery High
Hunts for the trojanised npm package postmark-mcp (backdoored at v1.0.16) landing in node_modules or being launched on a developer device. The malicious MCP server silently BCCs every outgoing email to phan@giftshop.club, so any presence of this exact package is a compromise indicator, not generic supply-chain noise. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious package name 'postmark-mcp' and its node_modules drop path named in the article ('first confirmed malicious MCP server ... blind-copying every outgoing email') — cross-checked against Koi Security, Snyk and The Hacker News, which confirm the v1.0.16 backdoor BCCing to phan@giftshop.club (the article IOC giftshop.club). Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/first-malicious-mcp-server-found.html • https://postmarkapp.com/blog/information-regarding-malicious-postmark-mcp-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1114 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst or AppSec engineer detonating/reviewing the sample in an isolated sandbox VM
  • An internal mirror/cache (Verdaccio, Artifactory) retaining a quarantined copy of the package for forensic review
  • A blocklist test where the package is intentionally installed to validate Aikido/EDR detection
  • A developer who pinned the legitimate Postmark official SDK but typo-named a local wrapper folder 'postmark-mcp'
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("MALWARE-SANDBOX","SECLAB","DETONATION"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the installed version from package.json/package-lock on the host — any version >=1.0.16 is backdoored. Confirm the file write was under an interactive developer account, not a CI runner. 2) Contain: remove the package, kill any running node MCP process, and rotate the Postmark Server API token plus any credentials/secrets that transited email while it was installed. 3) Hunt: search mail logs for BCC recipients @giftshop.club, and sweep all developer endpoints for the same node_modules\postmark-mcp path to scope blast radius.
let lookback = 30d;
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
 | where ProcessCommandLine has "postmark-mcp"
 | where AccountName !endswith "$"
 | extend Signal="process", Path=FolderPath, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine, Hash=SHA256),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
 | where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\postmark-mcp"
 | extend Signal="file", Path=FolderPath, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Hash=SHA256, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal, Path, Cmd, Hash
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
union
(ImFileEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
 | where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\postmark-mcp"
 | extend Signal="file", Path=TargetFilePath, Cmd=ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash=TargetFileSHA256, User=ActorUsername),
(ImProcessCreate
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
 | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "postmark-mcp" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "postmark-mcp" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "postmark-mcp"
 | extend Signal="process", Path=TargetProcessName, Cmd=TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash=SHA256, User=ActorUsername)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, User, Signal, Path, Cmd, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious postmark-mcp npm Package Dropped to node_modules
id: 6f3a1c2e-9b54-4d7a-8c11-2a0f5e7d9b01
description: Detects the trojanised postmark-mcp MCP server package (backdoored v1.0.16+) being written into a node_modules directory on a developer host. The package BCCs all outgoing email to phan@giftshop.club.
references:
  - https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft
  - https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1114
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\node_modules\postmark-mcp\'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon ((@EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\node_modules\\postmark-mcp\\* OR *\\node_modules\\Postmark-Mcp\\*)) OR (@EventID:1 @CommandLine:*postmark-mcp*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\node_modules\\postmark-mcp\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*postmark-mcp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` 
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*postmark-mcp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` 
| sort - lastTime
GlassWorm Stage-2 C2 beacon to Vultr-hosted command-and-control IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from developer endpoints to GlassWorm's confirmed C2 infrastructure (Vultr IPs 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255 and the payload/exfil host 217.69.3.152 serving /wall). GlassWorm backdoors VS Code / OpenVSX extensions, so the initiating process is typically Code.exe, an extension host, or node. Rationale: Pivots on GlassWorm's confirmed C2 IPs named in external write-ups (Koi/BleepingComputer/Truesec) — the article-provided IOCs 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157 and 70.34.242.255 are corroborated as Vultr C2, and 217.69.3.152/wall is the confirmed zipped-exfil endpoint. The article names the GlassWorm VS Code extension compromise explicitly. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/glassworm-botnet-disrupted-after-resilient-c2-infrastructure-takedown/ • https://www.truesec.com/hub/blog/glassworm-self-propagating-vscode-extension • https://www.veracode.com/blog/glassworm-vs-code-extension/ • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2026/03/glassworm-attack-installs-fake-browser-extension-for-surveillance
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vultr is shared hosting — after the March 2026 takedown these IPs may be reassigned to a benign tenant, producing stale-IOC hits
  • A red-team / pentest engagement that happens to stand up infrastructure on the same Vultr ranges
  • A developer browsing to an unrelated site now hosted on a recycled IP
  • A threat-intel sandbox or VirusTotal retro-hunt VM detonating the sample and beaconing out
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process — GlassWorm beacons originate from Code.exe, the extension host, or node; a browser hitting the IP is far lower priority. Check whether the host has recently installed/updated VS Code or OpenVSX extensions. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, block the four C2 IPs at the egress firewall, and disable/remove suspect extensions. 3) Hunt: enumerate installed VS Code/OpenVSX extensions for invisible-Unicode payloads, search for the Solana-wallet C2-resolution traffic and connections to 217.69.3.152/wall, and check for credential/crypto-wallet file access across other developer hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255","217.69.3.152")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255","217.69.3.152")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

Compromised Rust crate onering performs code exfiltration

Aikido
2026-06-10 7 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The compromised onering Rust crate v1.4.1 on crates.io shipped a malicious build.rs that exfiltrates the diff of your latest commit to a hosted Sentry endpoint every time you build. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002
Domainso4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Rust build script making outbound network connection (build-time exfil) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Exfiltration to attacker-controlled Sentry ingest endpoint (onering crate) · [LLM] Rust build script harvesting git commit diff (onering build.rs) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Exfiltration to attacker-controlled Sentry ingest endpoint (onering crate) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound traffic to the specific Sentry org/project used by the trojanised onering 1.4.1 crate to disguise stolen git diffs as crash telemetry. The org id o4511539639222272 / project 4511539669368912 is attacker-controlled, so any contact is high-fidelity regardless of which package or build host triggered it. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact attacker Sentry infrastructure (host o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io, project 4511539669368912/envelope). This org/project id is attacker-owned, so a match is not generic Sentry crash reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-rust-crate-onering-performs-code-exfiltration • https://intel.aikido.dev/malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/trapdoor-supply-chain-attack-spreads.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001 T1036
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the onering build inside a sandbox
  • EDR/CI detonation chamber building the crate for analysis
  • An internal app erroneously configured with this exact DSN (effectively impossible — org id is attacker-owned)
  • Legitimate Sentry telemetry to a DIFFERENT org/project (will not match this host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the build that resolved the domain; confirm a Cargo build was running and pull Cargo.lock to see if onering 1.4.1 (or a git pin of cenotelie/onering) is present. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io at egress/DNS, and treat the most recent commit diff as exfiltrated — rotate any secrets that appeared in recent commits. 3) Hunt: sweep all dev/CI hosts for the same domain and for onering 1.4.1 in lockfiles; review git history for what diffs would have leaked.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or RemoteUrl has "4511539669368912/envelope"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rust build script harvesting git commit diff (onering build.rs) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the onering build.rs collection step: a Rust build-script-build.exe spawning git to capture the latest commit's full diff and metadata. Anchored on the exact `git diff HEAD^ HEAD` and the malicious `--pretty=format:{"commit":"%H"...}` JSON template the payload uses. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim payload strings: `git diff HEAD^ HEAD` and the bespoke `--pretty=format:{"commit":"%H",...}` JSON, scoped to a Cargo build-script parent (build-script-build.exe / target dir), which is where the onering build.rs executes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-rust-crate-onering-performs-code-exfiltration • https://intel.aikido.dev/malware
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vergen / built / git-version build scripts running git log/describe to embed a commit hash (lacks diff HEAD^ HEAD)
  • A bespoke build.rs that generates a changelog from the last commit diff
  • CI build scripts that snapshot commit metadata for provenance
  • git invoked by an IDE/test harness that happens to run during a build
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("describe","rev-parse","rev-list","symbolic-ref") and ProcessCommandLine !contains "HEAD^ HEAD")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is a Cargo build script (build-script-build.exe under \target\...\build\) and check Cargo.lock for onering 1.4.1 or a cenotelie/onering git dependency. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the build, and assume the latest commit diff was exfiltrated — rotate secrets present in recent commits and block the Sentry endpoint. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC for network egress to o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io from the same host/time window, and sweep all dev/CI hosts for the same parent→git diff pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "git.exe"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "diff" and ProcessCommandLine contains "HEAD^ HEAD")
    or ProcessCommandLine contains '--pretty=format:{"commit":"%H"'
| where InitiatingProcessFileName endswith "build-script-build.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\target\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\git.exe"
| where (CommandLine has "diff" and CommandLine contains "HEAD^ HEAD")
    or CommandLine contains '--pretty=format:{"commit":"%H"'
| where ParentProcessName endswith "build-script-build.exe" or ParentProcessName has "\\target\\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rust build script making outbound network connection (build-time exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioral hunt for the onering exfil channel: a Cargo build-script-build.exe (or a curl child it spawns) opening a connection to a public host during compilation. Build scripts that phone home are abnormal; this catches the attack even if the C2 domain rotates, while keeping the known Sentry endpoint in scope. Rationale: Targets the article's core novelty — outbound traffic emitted from a Cargo build script (build-script-build.exe) / curl child during build — which is anomalous behavior; the Sentinel variant pins curl to the exact Sentry envelope endpoint strings from the payload. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-rust-crate-onering-performs-code-exfiltration • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/five-malicious-rust-crates-and-ai-bot.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1195.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • openssl-sys / libgit2-sys / cmake / protobuf-src build scripts downloading native dependencies at build time
  • Crates that fetch prebuilt binaries or vendored sources during build
  • Build scripts pulling from crates.io mirrors or a corporate proxy
  • cargo/rustup refreshing the registry index concurrently with a build
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("crates.io","static.crates.io","github.com","githubusercontent.com","sh.rustup.rs","pkg.go.dev") and not (RemoteUrl has "ingest.de.sentry.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the destination — if it is o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io (or any Sentry envelope path from a build script), escalate immediately; otherwise check whether the consuming crate legitimately downloads native deps. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the destination, and treat recent commit diffs as exfiltrated; pull Cargo.lock for onering 1.4.1. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC2 (git diff HEAD^ HEAD harvesting) on the same host/time, and baseline which build scripts in your CI legitimately egress to allow-list them.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName endswith "build-script-build.exe"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe","powershell.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName endswith "build-script-build.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has "ingest.de.sentry.io" or CommandLine has "/envelope/" or CommandLine has "x-sentry-envelope"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "build-script-build.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

10 year old critical vulnerability in phpBB affecting tens of millions of users across thousands of forums

Aikido
2026-06-10 6 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Aikido Security discovered a critical unauthenticated authentication bypass in phpBB affecting tens of millions of users. A single HTTP request is all it takes to take over any account — a vulnerability that's been sitting in the codebase since 2014. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposed phpBB instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-48611 / 48612 / 29199 auth bypass · [LLM] phpBB ACP access from a source IP with no prior login (CVE-2026-48611 session hijack) · [LLM] phpBB password-reset host-header poisoning (CVE-2026-29199) · [LLM] phpBB OAuth account-binding CSRF via cross-site request to /user/oauth/authenticate/ (CVE-2026-48612)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Exposed phpBB instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-48611 / 48612 / 29199 auth bypass AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed hosts running phpBB at or below 3.3.16 / 4.0.0-a2 that are exposed to the June 2026 unauthenticated session-hijack (CVE-2026-48611), OAuth CSRF binding (CVE-2026-48612) and password-reset host-header poisoning (CVE-2026-29199). This is the highest-value actionable item from a disclosure that withheld exploit strings: find the vulnerable forum software before an attacker does. Rationale: Anchored on the three confirmed CVE IDs (CVE-2026-48611 main auth bypass, CVE-2026-48612 OAuth CSRF, CVE-2026-29199 host-header reset) and the SoftwareName 'phpbb' fallback plus the fixed line 3.3.17 from the article. CVE IDs beyond the article's 29199 were obtained by cross-checking SentinelOne, Infosecurity Magazine and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29199/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/test or staging phpBB instances that are not internet-facing and lower risk
  • Scanner reports an old phpBB path left on disk after the live site was already upgraded to 3.3.17
  • phpBB bundled inside a vendor appliance the scanner version-detects but cannot patch independently
  • SoftwareName match catches unrelated 'phpBB Bridge' plugins rather than the core app
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is internet-facing and the detected version is truly <=3.3.16/4.0.0-a2 (check the live HTTP banner / styles version, not just on-disk files). 2) Contain: upgrade to 3.3.17 (or master for 4.x) immediately; if upgrade is delayed, apply the phpBB workaround and force-rotate all admin sessions/passwords since the bypass needs no creds. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host into UC2/UC3/UC4 web-log detections to determine whether the bypass, reset-poisoning or OAuth-binding was already exercised before patching.

phpBB ACP access from a source IP with no prior login (CVE-2026-48611 session hijack) AIExploitation Low
The CVE-2026-48611 bypass grants a valid session as any user (including admins) from a single unauthenticated request — so the attacker reaches the Admin Control Panel without ever POSTing credentials. This hunts access to phpBB adm/index.php from client IPs that never submitted a ucp.php login in the lookback window. Rationale: Uses phpBB-specific paths from the article's product context: the Admin Control Panel at adm/index.php and the login flow ucp.php?mode=login. Reaching the ACP with zero preceding login POST from the same IP is the post-exploitation tell of the credential-free CVE-2026-48611 bypass. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin with a persistent 'remember me' cookie who did not submit a fresh login POST inside the window
  • Admin behind a NAT/proxy whose ACP traffic egresses from a different IP than their original login
  • Monitoring/uptime tools or internal scanners that periodically GET adm/index.php
  • Load balancer or reverse proxy collapsing client IPs so the login and ACP request appear on different recorded src values
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: drop known monitoring egress IPs and remember-me sessions
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0")  // replace placeholder list with your uptime-monitor egress IPs after first triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the flagged IP — geolocation, user-agent, and whether it hit member-list / ucp.php first; legitimate admins almost always have a login or a long benign history. 2) Contain: invalidate all phpBB sessions (clear the sessions table / rotate the board's auth secret), force admin password resets, and block the IP at the WAF if foreign. 3) Hunt: review adm/ actions for new admin accounts, extension installs or board-config changes (the RCE path) and correlate the same IP against UC4 OAuth-binding activity.

phpBB password-reset host-header poisoning (CVE-2026-29199) AIExploitation Medium
CVE-2026-29199 lets an attacker inject a malicious Host header on a phpBB password-reset request (ucp.php?mode=sendpassword) so the emailed reset link points at an attacker domain, leaking the single-use token. This hunts sendpassword requests grouped by the Host header they carried, surfacing any host value that is not the board's canonical FQDN. Rationale: Anchored on phpBB's reset endpoint ucp.php?mode=sendpassword and the Host-header mechanic confirmed by the SentinelOne CVE-2026-29199 write-up. Grouping by CsHost (the Host header) makes the injected/foreign hostname the rare bucket an analyst eyeballs — no canonical FQDN needs to be hard-coded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29199/ • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multi-domain board legitimately served under several hostnames / vanity domains
  • Internal health checks or CDN edge nodes that send their own Host value on the reset endpoint
  • Staging hostname used during a migration that briefly co-exists with production
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites Host to an internal upstream name (e.g. localhost / app-internal)
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: keep only non-canonical hosts once your real FQDNs are known
| where CsHost !endswith "yourforum.example"  // append your legitimate board FQDNs after first review
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the rare CsHost / site values — any host that is not your board's official FQDN(s) on a sendpassword request is a poisoning attempt; capture the source IP and target username if logged. 2) Contain: set phpBB's force_server_vars / canonical server name so the reset URL ignores the client Host, upgrade to 3.3.17, and invalidate outstanding reset tokens for any targeted accounts. 3) Hunt: check whether the targeted account's reset token was subsequently consumed from a different IP, and review that account for ACP access (UC2).

| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SrcIPs=dcount(CIp), SampleIPs=make_set(CIp, 15) by CsHost, CsUriStem
| order by Requests asc

| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`

| sort + Requests

phpBB OAuth account-binding CSRF via cross-site request to /user/oauth/authenticate/ (CVE-2026-48612) AIExploitation Medium
CVE-2026-48612 chains CSRF with missing OAuth state validation so a victim merely loading an attacker page (e.g. an <img src> tag) silently binds the attacker's Google/Facebook/Bitly credential to the victim's phpBB account. This hunts requests to the phpBB OAuth authenticate endpoint whose Referer is an external site rather than a legitimate OAuth provider or the board itself. Rationale: Uses the exact OAuth endpoint /user/oauth/authenticate/ named in the article plus the <img src> CSRF delivery and provider list (Google/Facebook/Bitly) confirmed by Pentest-Tools and Infosecurity. Comparing the Referer host against the request's own CsHost and excluding real OAuth providers isolates the cross-site binding request with no hard-coded board domain. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User who started the OAuth flow from a legitimate third-party SSO portal whose host isn't in the provider exclusion list
  • Link shorteners or email-tracking redirectors that rewrite the Referer to their own domain
  • Board embedded in an iframe on a partner site that legitimately initiates OAuth login
  • Browser privacy settings stripping/altering Referer, producing odd RefHost values that aren't truly malicious
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: add your own SSO/redirector hosts to the allowlist once confirmed benign
| where RefHost !in~ ("sso.yourforum.example")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the flagged request — note the victim session/account it targeted, the attacker Referer host, and whether a new OAuth identity was linked immediately after. 2) Contain: upgrade to 3.3.17 (which moves and hardens the redirect handler at /user/oauth/authenticate/), unlink any unrecognised OAuth credentials from affected accounts, and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: enumerate all OAuth-link events in the same window for other victims, and cross-check whether any newly bound account then accessed the ACP (UC2).
AppServiceHTTPLogs

| where CsUriStem has "oauth/authenticate"
| where isnotempty(Referer)
| extend RefHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Referer).Host))
| where isnotempty(RefHost)
| where not(CsHost has RefHost) and not(RefHost has CsHost)
| where RefHost !in~ ("accounts.google.com","www.facebook.com","facebook.com","bitly.com","login.live.com","login.microsoftonline.com")
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, CsHost, RefHost, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, CsMethod, UserAgent, ScStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*oauth/authenticate*" by Web.src Web.site Web.uri_path Web.http_referrer Web.http_user_agent
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`

| where NOT match(http_referrer, "(?i)(google|facebook|bitly|live|microsoftonline)\\.com")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime by src site uri_path http_referrer http_user_agent
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*oauth/authenticate*" by Web.src Web.site Web.uri_path Web.http_referrer Web.http_user_agent
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`

Bun runtime executed from temp dir running _index.js payload (Hades Campaign) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Hades/Miasma supply-chain second stage: the Python import hook downloads a standalone Bun runtime into a temp 'b' directory and runs the malicious _index.js bundle via `bun run _index.js`. This is the article's most specific execution artifact and is unusual in any normal developer/CI environment. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim execution string `bun run _index.js` plus the standalone `bun` binary name from the deobfuscated import hook — the binary+args combination has no legitimate occurrence in normal environments. Detections built from article strings; no external IOC bundle located for this 2026 campaign.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running a project whose entry bundle is genuinely named _index.js via `bun run`
  • CI pipeline that builds with Bun and has a script step named 'run' touching an _index.js
  • Local benchmarking/testing of the Bun runtime by an engineer evaluating it
  • Monorepo tooling that invokes `bun run` against framework-generated _index.js artifacts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","pip","sh","bash") or FolderPath has "/b/bun"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm the parent is a python/python3 interpreter importing a package (site-packages path) and that the bun binary lives under a temp '/b/' directory rather than a project node_modules. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, kill the bun process, and remove /tmp/b/bun, /tmp/b.zip and the /tmp/.bun_ran flag file; rotate any cloud/CI secrets exposed to that runner. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package that triggered the import (ensmallen 0.8.101, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1, mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4) across all hosts and check for outbound GitHub exfil.

| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "run" and ProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "run" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

Scripting interpreter downloads Bun v1.3.14 runtime from oven-sh GitHub releases AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Hades delivery step where the Python hook calls urlretrieve to pull the pinned Bun runtime ZIP (bun-v1.3.14) from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases. The high-fidelity signal is a Python/Node interpreter (not a browser or package manager) fetching the platform-specific bun ZIP to bootstrap an out-of-band JS engine. Rationale: Uses the exact pinned download path from the deobfuscated hook — `github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.14/bun-{os}-{arch}.zip` — combined with a scripting-interpreter initiating process, which distinguishes malware bootstrap from a developer's browser download. Medium confidence because legitimate Bun adoption exists; pin on the interpreter parent + exact version path.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.006

CI runner secret theft via /proc/<pid>/mem read of Runner.Worker (Miasma memory scraper) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Miasma Linux memory-scraping technique carried into the Hades Campaign: a scripting interpreter walks /proc/<pid>/maps and reads /proc/<pid>/mem of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process to scrape plaintext secrets from memory. Targets the proc-filesystem credential access primitive directly. Rationale: Targets the article's named credential-access primitive — reading /proc/<pid>/mem of Runner.Worker to scrape plaintext secrets — anchored on the /proc/<pid>/mem path and a scripting-interpreter opener. Defender Advanced Hunting has no /proc read telemetry, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; detection is expressed on Falcon FileOpenInfo and Linux auditd/Syslog where the path is observable.
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Debuggers (gdb, lldb) or profilers legitimately reading /proc/<pid>/mem
  • Crash-dump/coredump tooling (e.g. core_pattern handlers, gcore)
  • Security/EDR agents or memory-forensics tools sampling process memory
  • Container runtime introspection reading process maps on a CI host
Suppression filter
| ContextImageFileName!=/(gdb|lldb|gcore|crash|systemd-coredump|strace)/i
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the reader process and the target PID — confirm the target is Runner.Worker (or another secret-bearing process) and that the reader is an unexpected python/bun spawned from a package import, not gdb/coredump tooling. 2) Contain: kill the reader, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret/token that runner had access to (cloud keys, GH tokens, registry creds). 3) Hunt: correlate with the bun bootstrap (`bun run _index.js`), /tmp/.bun_ran flag, and outbound GitHub exfil; expand to macOS runners for task_for_pid-based scraping by the same package set.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/proc/" and SyslogMessage has "/mem"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("python","bun","Runner.Worker")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'

Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack Targeting AI Coding Agents

StepSecurity
2026-06-09 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 5, 2026, the Miasma worm campaign reached Microsoft's Azure GitHub organizations. GitHub disabled 73 repositories across four Microsoft GitHub organizations after a malicious commit was pushed to the Azure/durabletask repository using a previously compromised contributor account. The attack planted configuration files that execute a credential-harvesting payload when a developer opens the repository in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Suspicious commit pattern: '[skip ci]' with backdated timestamp adding only IDE config files · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] node.exe spawned by Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini executing .github/setup.js · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositori
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's signature artifact: simultaneous creation of SessionStart hooks and folderOpen tasks in .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, and .vscode/tasks.json — all pointing at node .github/setup.js. This is the precise file-set planted in the June 5 2026 Azure/durabletask commit 5f456b8. Rationale: The five planted-file paths are verbatim from the article's 'Five Planted Files, Four Attack Vectors' section. Requiring >=2 co-occurrence per host suppresses single legitimate .vscode/tasks.json edits while keeping near-zero FP on the Miasma file-set. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/ • https://github.com/step-security/supply-chain-firewall
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer scaffolding a new repo with VS Code tasks.json AND committing a .vscode workspace file at the same time
  • Engineering platform team rolling out a corporate .cursor/rules/ template across repos
  • Repo containing legitimate .github/setup.js for project bootstrapping (rare; size + obfuscation differentiates)
  • Renovate/Dependabot edits to .vscode/tasks.json without other paired files (will not trigger >=2 threshold)
  • Developer copying a template repo locally that legitimately includes both .claude and .vscode dirs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","Code.exe","Cursor.exe") and array_length(ArtifactsSeen) == 1 and ArtifactsSeen has "vscode-folderopen")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess (typically git.exe / Code.exe checkout) and inspect the .github/setup.js size and entropy; the Miasma payload is exactly 4,643,745 bytes single-line obfuscated JS. Pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for any node.exe child within 60s. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill any node setup.js process tree, force-revoke the developer's GitHub PAT / OAuth tokens, cloud CLI tokens (aws, az, gcloud), and rotate any .npmrc / .pypirc / kubeconfig secrets that the harvester targets. Step 3 — Hunt: search the org for any repo containing the five planted paths via GitHub code-search API; check for outbound DNS to check.git-service.com / t.m-kosche.com / git-service.com from any developer endpoint in the past 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    FolderPath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    FolderPath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    FolderPath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2  // co-occurrence of >=2 of the 5 planted files
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    TargetFilePath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Miasma Worm AI-Agent Hook Config Planted
id: 8a2a4e0f-3d9c-4b7d-9b4f-1d2e7c61a210
description: Detects creation of SessionStart hooks / folderOpen tasks / Cursor prompt-injection rules that the Miasma worm plants in compromised repos to auto-execute node .github/setup.js when a developer opens the project in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-worm-hits-microsoft-again-azure-functions-action-and-72-other-repositories-disabled-after-supply-chain-attack-targeting-ai-coding-agents
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/06
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1546
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.claude\settings.json'
      - '\.gemini\settings.json'
      - '\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc'
      - '\.vscode\tasks.json'
      - '\.github\setup.js'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\.claude\\settings.json OR *\\.gemini\\settings.json OR *\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc OR *\\.vscode\\tasks.json OR *\\.github\\setup.js))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\\.(claude|gemini)\\\\settings\.json$|\\\.cursor\\\\rules\\\\setup\.mdc$|\\\.vscode\\\\tasks\.json$|\\\.github\\\\setup\.js$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(), collect(TargetFileName)])
| _count >= 2
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.claude\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.gemini\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.vscode\\tasks.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\setup.js") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where mvcount(paths)>=2
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.claude\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.gemini\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.vscode\\tasks.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\setup.js") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where mvcount(paths)>=2
node.exe spawned by Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini executing .github/setup.js AIExploitation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's automatic execution chain: VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, or Gemini CLI launching node.exe with .github/setup.js as the script argument. This is the runtime detonation produced when a developer simply opens a repo containing the planted hook configs. Rationale: Article quotes the exact command 'node .github/setup.js' invoked by all four planted configs (Claude SessionStart, Gemini SessionStart, Cursor prompt injection, VS Code folderOpen task). Anchoring on parent IDE + node.exe + setup.js path is high-fidelity because legitimate projects rarely store bootstrap scripts under .github/. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/ • https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/tasks#_run-behavior
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with a legitimate project-bootstrap node script genuinely under .github/setup.js
  • Internal devtools team running .github/setup.js via VS Code task as a sanctioned scaffold
  • CI runner image with cached IDE binaries executing setup scripts during build
  • Repo template repos where setup.js is an intentional installer
  • Security researcher analysing the Miasma sample in a sandbox (whitelist sandbox host IDs)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has "sandbox" or DeviceName has "malware-lab")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: hash the setup.js (expect 4,643,745 bytes / SHA256 mismatch to any known-good repo) and capture the first 1 KB of the single-line obfuscated JS for IR. Pull network egress from the node.exe PID. Step 2 — Contain: kill the node process tree, isolate the host, and revoke developer-context credentials — GitHub PAT/OAuth, AWS/Azure/GCP CLI tokens, kubeconfig, NPM/PyPI tokens, SSH keys (article confirms harvester targets AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes + 90+ dev tool configs). Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate all repos cloned on the host in the past 30 days and check each working tree for the five planted paths; sweep the org's GitHub for commits with message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext [skip ci]' or backdated commits to 2020-03-09.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts resolution or connection to the Miasma worm's credential-exfiltration infrastructure: check.git-service.com, git-service.com, and t.m-kosche.com. These domains receive harvested AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets from the planted payload. Rationale: Three domains are explicitly listed in the article's pre-extracted IOCs (check.git-service.com, t.m-kosche.com, git-service.com). Article says credential-harvesting payload exfiltrates AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets, so DNS+network egress to these domains is high-fidelity C2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-worm-hits-microsoft-again-azure-functions-action-and-72-other-repositories-disabled-after-supply-chain-attack-targeting-ai-coding-agents
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise self-hosted Git on a sub-domain that coincidentally matches *git-service.com (rare; whitelist by exact FQDN)
  • Threat-intel feed fetcher / sandbox detonation system (whitelist sandbox host IDs)
  • Security researcher visiting the domain for reverse-engineering
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ infrastructure resolving the indicator (whitelist sinkhole resolver IP)
  • Browsing to the StepSecurity blog post itself (won't hit subdomains directly)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sinkhole","sandbox","ti-fetcher"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the initiating process and user; if InitiatingProcessFileName is node.exe, immediately pivot to its command line for .github/setup.js. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, block the three domains at the corporate resolver and egress proxy, and treat all credentials accessible from the user/host context as compromised — rotate cloud tokens, GitHub PATs, NPM/PyPI/Cargo registry tokens, kubeconfig, SSH keys. Step 3 — Hunt: 30-day lookback across the entire fleet for any resolution of git-service.com or m-kosche.com; correlate hits with file-creation of .github/setup.js or the four IDE hook configs to find latent infections.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com") or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.git-service.com","t.m-kosche.com","git-service.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP, Domain = Name, QueryType = QueryTypeName, Result),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = SrcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DnsQuery, QueryType = DnsQueryTypeName, Result = DnsResponseCodeName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationDnsDomain has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com") or RequestURL has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), QueryType = "proxy", Result = DeviceAction)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious commit pattern: '[skip ci]' with backdated timestamp adding only IDE config files AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Miasma commit fingerprint: a single push where 5 files added / 0 source files modified, commit message ends with '[skip ci]', author date backdated to a pre-2024 timestamp, and the added paths include AI-agent config dirs. Detects via GitHub Audit Log shipped to Sentinel/Defender via CloudAppEvents or to Datadog via the GitHub integration. Rationale: Article details the exact commit fingerprint: commit 5f456b8 with message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext [skip ci]', 5 files added / 0 source files modified, backdated to 2020-03-09T15:59:47Z (six years before push). The conjunction of [skip ci] + backdated author date + added IDE-config paths is the Miasma operator signature. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/admin/monitoring-activity-in-your-enterprise/reviewing-audit-logs-for-your-enterprise
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate maintainer importing an old Git history with [skip ci] in a merge commit
  • Repository migration from another VCS preserving original author dates pre-2024
  • CI maintenance commit adding .vscode/tasks.json with [skip ci] (will not match >=2 of the IDE paths usually)
  • Bot commits (Renovate/Dependabot) with skip-ci that touch tasks.json
  • Developer rebasing old branches with preserved author timestamps
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the actor account from the audit event, check its recent activity for token regeneration / SSH key additions / new OAuth grants; correlate against the May 19 PyPI durabletask incident actor. Step 2 — Contain: suspend the GitHub account, revoke all PATs and OAuth grants, force-rotate any GitHub App / Action secrets the account had access to, and revert the commit from any affected default branches. Step 3 — Hunt: GitHub code-search the org for any other repos containing the five planted paths or the commit message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext'; query GitHub Audit Log for the same actor across all owned orgs for [skip ci] commits adding files outside src trees.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "GitHub"
| where ActionType in ("Repositories.Push","RepositoriesPush","git.push")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "[skip ci]"
| where Raw has_any (".claude/settings.json",".gemini/settings.json",".cursor/rules/setup.mdc",".vscode/tasks.json",".github/setup.js")
| extend AuthorDate = extract(@"author[^\d]+(\d{4})-\d{2}-\d{2}", 1, Raw)
| where isnotempty(AuthorDate) and toint(AuthorDate) < 2024
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ObjectName, AuthorDate, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires GitHub Audit Log connector (GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL) or CommonSecurityLog ingest
GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where action_s == "git.push" or action_s == "repo.push"
| where commits_s has "[skip ci]"
| where commits_s has_any (".claude/settings.json",".gemini/settings.json",".cursor/rules/setup.mdc",".vscode/tasks.json",".github/setup.js")
| extend AuthorYear = extract(@"author[^\d]+(\d{4})-\d{2}-\d{2}", 1, commits_s)
| where isnotempty(AuthorYear) and toint(AuthorYear) < 2024
| project TimeGenerated, actor_s, actor_ip_s, repo_s, commits_s, AuthorYear
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:github @evt.name:git.push @commits.message:*"[skip ci]"* (@commits.added:(*.claude/settings.json* OR *.gemini/settings.json* OR *.cursor/rules/setup.mdc* OR *.vscode/tasks.json* OR *.github/setup.js*))
CLOUD
`github_audit` action=git.push | spath input=raw_event | search commits{}.message="*[skip ci]*" (commits{}.added{}="*.claude/settings.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.gemini/settings.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.cursor/rules/setup.mdc" OR commits{}.added{}="*.vscode/tasks.json" OR commits{}.added{}="*.github/setup.js") | eval author_year=substr('commits{}.timestamp',1,4) | where author_year<"2024" | table _time repo actor commits{}.id commits{}.message commits{}.added{} author_year
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
